questions.prompt: A startup's leadership decides not to buy on-premises servers for its new project, and instead provisions Azure VMs sized for current needs, paying only for what it actually uses each month. Which best describes what this represents?
options: A shift from CapEx to OpEx — infrastructure spending becomes an ongoing, variable cost instead of a large upfront purchase that depreciates over years
A shift from OpEx to CapEx, since a recurring cloud bill is still a capital expense
No real financial difference from buying hardware outright — it's just renamed
A shift that only changes accounting categorization, with no actual effect on cash flow timing
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines this exact shift: CapEx is a large upfront purchase that depreciates over years, while OpEx is an ongoing, variable cost that scales with actual use. Renting sized-for-now VMs and paying by usage is the textbook move from CapEx to OpEx — which is why a company can also shut off a cancelled project's compute costs the same day, something buying hardware outright never allowed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: scaling a resource up to handle a traffic spike, then scaling it back down afterward while paying only for what's actually used, is the cloud characteristic Lesson 1 calls rapid ________.
questions.explain: Rapid elasticity is one of the five defining characteristics of cloud computing from Lesson 1's table: scale up for a spike, scale back down after, and pay only for what's actually used in the meantime.

questions.prompt: Match each service model to its Azure example and what Microsoft manages, per Lesson 2.
right: Microsoft manages the entire stack including the application itself — example: Microsoft 365
Microsoft manages hardware and virtualization only; you manage the OS up — example: Virtual Machines
Microsoft manages hardware, virtualization, the OS, and the runtime; you manage just your app and data — example: Azure App Service
questions.explain: IaaS (Virtual Machines) stops Microsoft's responsibility at virtualization, leaving the OS up to you. PaaS (App Service) extends Microsoft's responsibility through the OS and runtime, leaving just your app and data. SaaS (Microsoft 365) means Microsoft manages the entire stack, including the application — you just use it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure regions and availability zones, per Lesson 3.
options: An availability zone is a physically separate datacenter within a region, with its own power, cooling, and networking
Every Azure region has at least three availability zones, with no exceptions
Spreading a resource across multiple availability zones protects against a single datacenter's power or cooling failure taking the whole application down
Choosing the region closest to a company's users is the only real consideration — compliance never factors into region choice
Data residency requirements can require data to physically stay within a specific country or region, regardless of where a company's users actually are
questions.explain: An availability zone is exactly a physically separate datacenter with its own power/cooling/network, and spreading resources across zones protects against one zone's failure taking everything down. Data residency rules can force data to stay within a region's borders regardless of user location. Lesson 3 is explicit that not every region has availability zones yet — it's a per-region capability, not a universal guarantee — and that latency and compliance are both real reasons to pick a region, not just proximity.

questions.prompt: A team created a resource group months ago as a quick sandbox for testing, and it now holds a VM, a storage account, and a VNet that nobody uses anymore. What's the fastest single action to remove all three, and what's the real risk that comes with that convenience?
options: Delete the resource group itself — every resource inside it is deleted along with it, so it's worth double-checking nothing inside is actually still needed before doing it
Delete each resource individually from inside the group first; deleting the group itself only removes its name, leaving the resources behind
Deleting a resource group only works once it's already completely empty
There's no way to remove multiple resources at once in Azure — each one must be deleted individually regardless of grouping
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is direct about this: deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it in one action. That's exactly what makes resource groups useful for tearing down a whole test environment fast — and exactly why it's also the fast way to lose something you didn't mean to, so confirming what's actually inside first matters.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for finding a specific resource you created last week without browsing through menus, per Lesson 4.
items: Open the Azure Portal at portal.azure.com
Press Ctrl+/ (or Cmd+/ on Mac) to jump to the global search bar
Type the resource's name, or the service it belongs to, into the search bar
Select the matching result from the search suggestions
Review the resource's blade, starting with its Overview
questions.explain: Lesson 4 specifically calls out the global search bar and its Ctrl+/ shortcut as faster than navigating menus once you've created more than a handful of resources: open the portal, jump to search, type the resource or service name, pick the match, and land on its blade's Overview.

questions.prompt: Which Azure storage service is purpose-built for unstructured files — images, video, log files, backups — and built to scale to enormous amounts of data cheaply?
options: Blob Storage
Azure Files
Azure Virtual Machine disk storage
Microsoft Entra ID
Azure Monitor
A Storage Account's access tier setting
questions.explain: Blob Storage ('Binary Large Object') is exactly the service Lesson 7 describes for unstructured data at scale — images, video, documents, log files, backups — built to be cheap at enormous scale.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B, Azure Files, is the closest wrong answer because it's also a storage service living inside the same Storage Account. But Azure Files is built for managed, SMB-accessible file shares that multiple machines can mount simultaneously like a network drive — not the cheap, massively scalable unstructured-file storage that Blob Storage specifically provides.

questions.prompt: A team needs to run a legacy Windows application that requires a specific, older OS configuration no PaaS runtime offers. Based on Lesson 6, what should they use, and why won't App Service work?
options: An Azure Virtual Machine — VMs are IaaS, so the team controls the OS itself, while App Service only runs supported, managed runtimes with no OS-level access
Azure App Service, since App Service can be configured to run any OS version a customer requests
Microsoft 365, since it's SaaS and requires no OS management at all
Azure Monitor, since it's the service responsible for choosing which OS a workload runs on
questions.explain: Lesson 6 draws this exact line: a VM gives full OS-level control because it's IaaS, which is precisely what you need for a legacy app with a specific, older OS dependency. App Service is PaaS — Microsoft manages the OS and runtime for you, which means you never get OS-level access to configure in the first place, so a legacy OS requirement simply can't be met there.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Azure Files provides managed file shares accessible over the standard ________ protocol, the same way a traditional on-premises network drive works.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 describes Azure Files as fully managed file shares accessible the same way an on-premises file share is — over the standard SMB protocol — letting multiple machines mount and read/write the same share.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Virtual Networks (VNets) and subnets, per Lesson 8.
options: A VNet is Azure's private, isolated network, and by default nothing outside it can reach resources inside it directly
Subnets let you apply different network rules to different parts of your infrastructure instead of treating the whole VNet as one flat space
Resources inside the same VNet communicate over the public internet, the same way resources in two different VNets would
The main value of a VNet is connectivity between resources — isolation is just an incidental side effect, not the actual point
A subnet is a smaller IP address range within a VNet, often used to separate resources by role, like web, app, and data tiers
questions.explain: A VNet really is private and isolated by default, and subnets really do let you apply different rules to different tiers, segmented by role and IP range. Lesson 8 is explicit that resources in the same VNet talk to each other using private IPs without that traffic ever going out over the public internet — the opposite of option C — and that isolation, not just connectivity, is actually the main point of a VNet, the opposite of option D.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure Monitor term to what it actually is, per Lesson 10.
right: A rule that notifies you or triggers an action when a defined condition is met
Azure's platform-wide observability service, collecting data automatically from almost every resource
A numerical value collected at regular intervals, like CPU percentage on a VM
A detailed, timestamped record of an event, richer than a single number
questions.explain: Azure Monitor is the platform-wide observability service itself. A metric is a numerical value sampled over time, like CPU percentage. A log is a detailed, timestamped record of an event. An alert is the rule that watches metrics or logs and notifies you when a defined condition is met.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difference between Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Azure Policy?
options: RBAC controls who can do what; Azure Policy controls what's allowed to exist at all, regardless of who's creating it
RBAC and Azure Policy are two different names for the exact same underlying system
Azure Policy controls who can do what; RBAC controls what's allowed to exist at all, regardless of who's creating it
RBAC only applies at the subscription scope, while Azure Policy only applies at the resource group scope
Azure Policy replaces the need for authentication, while RBAC replaces the need for authorization
RBAC enforces region restrictions on deployments, while Azure Policy manages role assignments
questions.explain: Lesson 13 draws this line directly: RBAC (Lesson 11) controls who can do what, while Azure Policy controls what's allowed to exist at all, regardless of who's creating it — a policy can block a non-compliant deployment even for someone with full Contributor rights.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C swaps the two systems' jobs exactly backwards — it's Azure Policy that controls what's allowed to exist regardless of who's creating it, and RBAC that controls who can do what. Reversing which system does which job is precisely the mix-up Lesson 13 warns against.

questions.prompt: A reporting analyst only needs to view cost data for one team's resource group — nothing else. Per the principle of least privilege from Lesson 11, what's the right role assignment?
options: The Reader role, scoped to just that one resource group
The Owner role, scoped to the whole subscription, so they're covered for anything they might need later
The Contributor role, scoped to the whole subscription
The Owner role, scoped to that resource group, since viewing costs requires managing billing settings too
questions.explain: Lesson 11's example is almost exactly this one: a reporting analyst who only needs to view cost data gets Reader at the resource group scope, not Owner at the subscription scope. Least privilege means the smallest role and narrowest scope that still lets the identity do its actual job — viewing never requires Owner or Contributor, and nothing here requires subscription-wide access.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Policy, tags, and management groups, per Lesson 13.
options: A policy with a "deny" effect blocks a non-compliant deployment outright
A policy with an "audit" effect just flags violations without blocking them
Tags change how a resource actually functions internally, not just how it's found, grouped, or billed
A management group sits above subscriptions, letting RBAC and Policy applied there flow down to every subscription beneath it automatically
Tags are unrelated to Cost Management's "accountability" principle from Lesson 12
questions.explain: Deny and audit are exactly the two policy effects Lesson 13 describes — one blocks, one just flags. A management group does sit above subscriptions so a policy applied once flows down automatically, mirroring the resource-group nesting from Lesson 5. Tags don't change how a resource works at all — they change how you can find, group, and bill it later — and they're specifically how Cost Management's accountability principle gets implemented, not unrelated to it.

questions.prompt: Match each compliance framework to what it addresses, per Lesson 14.
right: US regulation on protecting health information
An auditor's report on security, availability, and confidentiality controls
EU regulation on personal data privacy and protection
An international standard for information security management systems
questions.explain: SOC 2 is an auditor's report on security, availability, and confidentiality controls. ISO 27001 is an international standard for information security management systems. GDPR is the EU's personal data privacy regulation. HIPAA is the US regulation covering health information — exactly Lesson 14's table.

questions.prompt: Put these containers in order from broadest (applies to the most subscriptions at once) down to narrowest, per Lesson 13's governance hierarchy.
questions.explain: Lesson 13's nesting diagram runs management groups above subscriptions, subscriptions above resource groups, and resource groups above individual resources — a policy or role applied at the management group level flows all the way down through every level beneath it.

questions.prompt: A developer runs `az group create --name rg-demo --location eastus` for the third time, using the exact same command and parameters each time. What happens on this third run, and why does that property actually matter for automation?
options: It still succeeds and produces the identical result as the first run — the CLI is repeatable, so the same command always produces the same outcome rather than erroring or creating duplicates
It fails on the second and third runs, because Azure refuses to create a resource group with a name that's already in use
It creates a second, separate resource group with a number automatically appended to the name
It succeeds, but the region silently changes to Azure's default region on each additional run
questions.explain: Lesson 15 calls this out directly as repeatability: running the same command the tenth time creates exactly the same thing as the first, with no chance of a misclick-driven difference. That's exactly why a CLI command is safe to save and rerun as part of an automated pipeline, unlike clicking through the Portal from memory.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Bicep is a friendlier language that compiles down to the exact same ________ underneath — nothing is lost or different at deployment time.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 is explicit that Bicep isn't a different underlying system — it compiles down to the exact same ARM JSON that Azure Resource Manager actually deploys. Bicep is simply a nicer way to author the same result.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order they actually happen when a resource is created, whether through the Portal or the CLI, per Lesson 17.
items: Your request (Portal click or CLI command) reaches Azure Resource Manager
Resource Manager checks your RBAC permissions at that scope
Resource Manager validates the request and provisions the resource
The resource becomes visible and billable
questions.explain: Lesson 17 walks through this sequence explicitly: both the Portal and the CLI are two front doors to the same process — the request reaches Resource Manager, Resource Manager checks RBAC permissions, validates and provisions the resource, and only then does it become visible and billable.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of `az group create --name rg-demo --location eastus` to what it means, per Lesson 15.
right: A parameter specifying which region to use
A parameter specifying what to name the resource group
The action — create a resource group
questions.explain: Lesson 15 breaks this exact command apart piece by piece: `az` calls the Azure CLI, `group create` is the action, `--name rg-demo` is the parameter naming the resource group, and `--location eastus` is the parameter choosing the region — the same `az <service> <action> --<parameter> <value>` shape almost every Azure CLI command follows.
